archetype.name: Playoff Team (puck-possession)
archetype.definition: A team that controls the puck and the chances at 5-on-5 well enough to win most nights, with a record so far that understates its play rather than overstating it.

report.headline: The control game is back; the saves haven't fully caught up yet
report.take:
Florida spent last season looking like a team whose window had shut. It went 40-38-4 for 84 points, finished 23rd on the site, and lost the 5-on-5 chance battle with a 49.3% xGF. Nine games into 2026-27 the old profile is back. Florida owns 58% of the shot attempts (3rd in the league) and 55.8% of the expected goals (6th), and it gives up only 23.9 shots a game. That is the possession team that went 52-24-6 and 47-31-4 in its contending years, when its xGF sat around 54-56%. The 5-2-2 start, a 109-point pace and the site's 6th spot come mostly from that, not from bounces.

The record has nothing inflated in it. Pts vs Goal Diff is a neutral +0.4, the 5-on-5 PDO is 99.5, and team save percentage is .888, 19th and below the league's .893. Shooting is ordinary at 11.4%, almost exactly the league rate. A team out-chancing opponents this badly with average finishing and below-average saves usually gets better results over time, not worse. Four of the nine games went past regulation, and the first stretch was a run of 1-0, 2-3 and 1-4 games before the offense opened up.

The raw numbers hide one wrinkle: the last five games ran hot at both ends. Florida scored 4.4 a game but allowed 3.4, which is 0.62 more than its season rate. Two blowouts of Columbus and Seattle cover some sloppy nights. Ekblad sits at -5 while carrying a 67% xGF, which looks like bad luck in goal rather than bad hockey. Sam Reinhart is the other oddity: 5 goals and 5 PP points, but a 40.4% xGF at 5-on-5, by far the worst among the top forwards. The engine is the two Tkachuks, 4th and 7th on the left-wing tab, with Matthew at 14 points. Behind them, Seth Jones is logging 25.5 minutes a night and has 10 points of his own.

The direction is up. If Markstrom keeps his slightly-positive GSAx and the depth goaltending stops costing goals, this is a top-eight team on process. Last year's collapse looks more like the outlier than the new baseline.

strengths.title: Owning the puck at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Florida leads its games in shot attempts and expected goals by wide margins, and its forwards nearly all post xGF shares near or above 60%. That has been the identity of every good Panthers season in the history block, so it reads as structural rather than a hot week. It is the main reason to trust this start.

strengths.title: Starving opponents of shots
strengths.body: Florida allows 23.9 shots a game, 2.4 fewer than the league average. The defense also holds opposing defensemen and wingers under their expected points. Long possession shifts mean less time defending, so this should hold as long as the puck-control numbers do.

strengths.title: Tkachuk-driven top end
strengths.body: Brady Tkachuk (6 goals, 32 shots) and Matthew Tkachuk (14 points, 59.8% xGF) are both top-seven on the left-wing tab. Seth Jones gives the blueline a true driver at 25.5 minutes a night. Their scoring comes with strong underlying shares, so it is not finishing luck.

concerns.title: Saves lag the shot suppression
concerns.body: Team save percentage is .888, below the league's .893, even though Florida faces few shots. Markstrom has been fine at .897 with a positive GSAx. Schmid's .878 and -0.6 GSAx across three starts are what drag the number down. This is the most fixable flaw, and it matters most on back-to-backs.

concerns.title: Leakier lately
concerns.body: The last five games brought 3.4 goals against a game, worse than the season rate, despite the shot suppression holding. Part of this is goaltending and part is game state in blowouts. If it continues against stronger opponents, it turns into a real structural issue.

concerns.title: Reinhart's chances run backwards
concerns.body: Reinhart plays the most minutes among the forwards and produces on the power play. At 5-on-5, though, his line owns only 40.4% of the expected goals, which stands out on a team this dominant. His goals may cool if the even-strength play doesn't improve.

trend.note: The season opened with a string of one-goal and overtime games and very little scoring. The last five turned into track meets: 22 goals for and 17 against, with more scoring but a slightly lower points percentage than the season as a whole.

weekAhead.headline: Four road games, three opponents who lose the puck battle
weekAhead.body:
All four games are on the road, which is the main drag. On the ice, the slate suits Florida. Ottawa, Chicago and Winnipeg all sit below 50% in xGF, and Chicago is near the bottom of the league on every axis. Pittsburgh is the outlier: a 3-5-1 team that actually wins the chance battle at 54.1%. Its weak goaltending and a soft defense against wingers make it beatable rather than dangerous.

The trap games are the two with records propped up by luck. Ottawa (+1.6 Pts vs Goal Diff, .910 save %) and Winnipeg (+1.4) have both outrun their play. Ottawa's A- goaltending is the likeliest thing to steal a game from a team that should dominate possession, and Winnipeg's 30% power play punishes undisciplined nights.

keyMatchups.title: Tkachuks against soft wing coverage
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa, Pittsburgh and Chicago all rank 27th or worse at limiting wingers' points against expectation. Florida's two best forwards are left wings. This is where the week's scoring should come from.

keyMatchups.title: Possession against Ottawa's goalie
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa gets out-attempted badly with a 44% CF, but its goaltending grades A- and stops .910. Florida should tilt the ice heavily. Whether that becomes goals depends on beating a goalie who has been carrying his team.

keyMatchups.title: Middling PK against Winnipeg's PP
keyMatchups.body: Winnipeg's power play converts at 30%, 3rd in the league. Florida's 80.6% kill is only mid-pack. Staying out of the box in the week's last game matters more than anywhere else on the trip.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts the back-to-back at Ottawa and Pittsburgh. A Schmid start against a soft Pittsburgh team is the test of whether the depth goaltending can hold up.

restOfSeason.body:
The possession numbers are the most durable part of this team, and they match Florida's contending seasons rather than last year's slide. Expect the 109-point pace to settle somewhat, because no team keeps a nine-game rate. The underlying play still supports a comfortable playoff season and a goal differential that should grow rather than shrink. Shooting is already average and Pts vs Goal Diff is neutral, so there is little luck to give back.

The upside lever is goaltending. If team save percentage drifts toward league average behind Markstrom, goals against should fall well into the top ten. If the backup role keeps leaking, Florida stays a good-not-great team that wins the shot clock and loses some games it controlled. The Atlantic is crowded early, but Florida's process is better than most of the teams ahead of it.
swingFactors: Team save % climbing to league average

confidence.note: Nine games is a small sample, but the shot-share numbers stabilize quickly and match the team's pre-2025-26 history.
